title: Stage Capabilities: Link Target
summary: This sub technique covers preparing the destination that a phishing link points to. The resource is usually a web page hosted on attacker controlled or compromised infrastructure, and it commonly clones the login page of a mail provider, a virtual private network portal, or a single sign on service so harvested credentials are typed into a convincing form. The page may include client side script that decides what each visitor sees, redirecting security scanners and automated crawlers away from the credential form while serving it to a real browser. Adversaries frequently register domains that resemble the target's real domain through typosquatting, homoglyph substitution, or a different top level domain, and they may hide the true destination behind shorteners, open redirects on trusted sites, or long query strings. Detection relies on newly registered domain feeds, proxy logs showing requests to lookalike host names, and user reports of a page that asks for a password after an unexpected link.

beginner.definition: A link target is the web page a link takes you to. An attacker builds that page before sending the link. It often copies a real login page so that you type your password into it. The copy sends your password to the attacker. This is one part of a wider idea called staging capabilities, where an attacker prepares everything before the attack starts.
beginner.whyItMatters: One stolen password can open mail, file storage, and many other systems. People trust login pages they recognise, so a good copy is hard to spot. Links also arrive through chat and text, not only email. Training users to check the address bar is not enough on its own.
howItWorks: The attacker registers a domain name that looks close to a real one.
They copy the real login page and place their own copy on that domain.
The copy sends anything you type to the attacker instead of the real service.
They add code that shows the page to real visitors but not to security scanners.
The link itself may be shortened or wrapped so the true address is hidden.
They send the link in an email, a chat message, or a text message.
beginner.example: Think of a post office with two counters that look identical. The real counter stamps your letter and sends it on. A second counter, opened next door with almost the same sign, takes your letter and your payment and quietly keeps both. Regular customers check the sign rather than the house number. The fake counter was built and staffed long before any customer was told to go there.
takeaways: A phishing link only works because a page was prepared in advance.
The copy of a login page sends your password straight to the attacker.
Lookalike domain names are the main clue you can spot by eye.

objectives: Describe what resources an attacker stages before sending a phishing link.
Explain how a cloned login page captures credentials.
Recognise lookalike domain patterns used to make a link plausible.
Identify proxy and domain registration data that reveals staged link targets.
Explain why shorteners and open redirects hide the true destination.
